**University College London** , which [operates as](/wiki/Trade_name "Trade
name") **UCL** ,[8][9][1] is a [public](/wiki/Public_university "Public
university") [research university](/wiki/Research_university "Research
university") in London, England. It is a [member
institution](/wiki/Member_institutions_of_the_University_of_London "Member
institutions of the University of London") of the
[federal](/wiki/Federal_university "Federal university") [University of
London](/wiki/University_of_London "University of London"), and is the second-
largest [university in the United Kingdom by total
enrolment](/wiki/List_of_universities_in_the_United_Kingdom_by_enrolment "List
of universities in the United Kingdom by enrolment")[6] and the largest by
postgraduate enrolment.

Established in 1826 as **London University** (although without university
status or degree-awarding powers) by founders who were inspired by the radical
ideas of [Jeremy Bentham](/wiki/Jeremy_Bentham "Jeremy Bentham"), UCL was the
first university institution to be established in London, and the first in
England to be entirely secular and to admit students regardless of their
religion.[10][11] It was also, in 1878, among the first university colleges to
admit women alongside men, two years after [University College,
Bristol](/wiki/University_College,_Bristol "University College, Bristol"), had
done so.[12] Intended by its founders to be [England's third
university](/wiki/Third-oldest_university_in_England_debate "Third-oldest
university in England debate"), politics forced it to accept the status of a
college in 1836, when it received a [royal charter](/wiki/Royal_charter "Royal
charter") and became one of the two founding [colleges of the University of
London](/wiki/Colleges_of_the_University_of_London "Colleges of the University
of London"), although it achieved _de facto_ recognition as a university in
the 1990s and formal university status in 2023. It has grown through mergers,
including with the [Institute of
Ophthalmology](/wiki/UCL_Institute_of_Ophthalmology "UCL Institute of
Ophthalmology") (in 1995), the [Institute of
Neurology](/wiki/UCL_Institute_of_Neurology "UCL Institute of Neurology") (in
1997), the [Royal Free Hospital](/wiki/Royal_Free_Hospital "Royal Free
Hospital") Medical School (in 1998), the [Eastman Dental
Institute](/wiki/UCL_Eastman_Dental_Institute "UCL Eastman Dental Institute")
(in 1999), the [School of Slavonic and East European
Studies](/wiki/UCL_School_of_Slavonic_and_East_European_Studies "UCL School of
Slavonic and East European Studies") (in 1999), the [School of
Pharmacy](/wiki/UCL_School_of_Pharmacy "UCL School of Pharmacy") (in 2012) and
the [Institute of Education](/wiki/UCL_Institute_of_Education "UCL Institute
of Education") (in 2014).

UCL has its main campus in the [Bloomsbury](/wiki/Bloomsbury "Bloomsbury") and
[St Pancras](/wiki/St_Pancras,_London "St Pancras, London") areas of [central
London](/wiki/Central_London "Central London"), with a number of institutes
and teaching hospitals elsewhere in central London and has a second campus,
[UCL East](/wiki/UCL_East "UCL East"), at [Queen Elizabeth Olympic
Park](/wiki/Queen_Elizabeth_Olympic_Park "Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park") in
[Stratford](/wiki/Stratford,_London "Stratford, London"), East London. UCL is
organised into 11 constituent faculties, within which there are over 100
departments, institutes and research centres. UCL operates several museums and
collections in a wide range of fields, including the [Petrie Museum of
Egyptian Archaeology](/wiki/Petrie_Museum_of_Egyptian_Archaeology "Petrie
Museum of Egyptian Archaeology") and the [Grant Museum of Zoology and
Comparative Anatomy](/wiki/Grant_Museum_of_Zoology_and_Comparative_Anatomy
"Grant Museum of Zoology and Comparative Anatomy"), and administers the annual
[Orwell Prize](/wiki/Orwell_Prize "Orwell Prize") in political writing. In
2023/24, UCL had a total income of £2.03 billion, of which £538.8 million was
from research grants and contracts.[2] The university generates around £10
billion annually for the UK economy, primarily through the spread of its
research and knowledge (£4 billion) and the impact of its own spending (£3
billion).[13]

UCL is a member of numerous academic organisations, including the [Russell
Group](/wiki/Russell_Group "Russell Group") and the [League of European
Research Universities](/wiki/League_of_European_Research_Universities "League
of European Research Universities"), and is part of [UCL
Partners](/wiki/UCL_Partners "UCL Partners"), the world's largest [academic
health science centre](/wiki/Academic_health_science_centre "Academic health
science centre").[14] It is considered part of the "[golden
triangle](/wiki/Golden_triangle_\(universities\) "Golden triangle
\(universities\)")" of research-intensive universities in southeast
England.[15] UCL has publishing and commercial activities including UCL Press,
[UCL Business](/wiki/UCL_Business "UCL Business") and UCL Consultants.

UCL has many notable alumni, including the founder of
[Mauritius](/wiki/Mauritius "Mauritius"), the [first prime minister of
Japan](/wiki/It%C5%8D_Hirobumi "Itō Hirobumi"), [one of the co-
discoverers](/wiki/Francis_Crick "Francis Crick") of the structure of
[DNA](/wiki/DNA "DNA"), and the members of [Coldplay](/wiki/Coldplay
"Coldplay"). UCL academics discovered five of the naturally occurring [noble
gases](/wiki/Noble_gases "Noble gases"), discovered [hormones](/wiki/Hormone
"Hormone"), invented the [vacuum tube](/wiki/Vacuum_tube "Vacuum tube"), and
made several [foundational advances](/wiki/History_of_statistics "History of
statistics") in modern statistics. As of 2025, 33 [Nobel
Prize](/wiki/Nobel_Prize "Nobel Prize") laureates[16] and three [Fields
medallists](/wiki/Fields_medal "Fields medal")[17] have been affiliated with
UCL as alumni or academic staff.

### 1826 to 1836 – London University

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=University_College_London&action=edit&section=2
"Edit section: 1826 to 1836 – London University")]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/78/University_of_London_1829.jpg/250px-
University_of_London_1829.jpg)](/wiki/File:University_of_London_1829.jpg)Share
no. 1105 in the University of London, issued 3 February 1829
[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/db/The_London_University_by_Thomas_Hosmer_Shepherd_1827-28.JPG/250px-
The_London_University_by_Thomas_Hosmer_Shepherd_1827-28.JPG)](/wiki/File:The_London_University_by_Thomas_Hosmer_Shepherd_1827-28.JPG)_The
London University_ (now the [UCL Main Building](/wiki/UCL_Main_Building "UCL
Main Building")) as imagined by [Thomas Hosmer
Shepherd](/wiki/Thomas_Hosmer_Shepherd "Thomas Hosmer Shepherd") in 1827–28,
when construction was in progress. The portico and dome were completed in
1829, but lack of funds meant it would be many years before reality matched
the picture.

UCL was founded on 11 February 1826 as an alternative to the
[Anglican](/wiki/Anglican "Anglican") universities of
[Oxford](/wiki/University_of_Oxford "University of Oxford") and
[Cambridge](/wiki/University_of_Cambridge "University of Cambridge").[18] It
took the form of a [joint stock company](/wiki/Joint_stock_company "Joint
stock company"), with shares sold for £100 (equivalent to £10,600 in 2023) to
proprietors, under the name of _London University_ , although without legal
recognition as a university or the associated right to award
degrees.[19][20][21] London University's first warden was [Leonard
Horner](/wiki/Leonard_Horner "Leonard Horner"), who was the first scientist to
head a British university.[22]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/60/Four_founders_of_UCL.JPG/250px-
Four_founders_of_UCL.JPG)](/wiki/File:Four_founders_of_UCL.JPG)[Henry
Tonks](/wiki/Henry_Tonks "Henry Tonks")' 1923 mural _The Four Founders of UCL_

Despite the commonly held belief that the philosopher [Jeremy
Bentham](/wiki/Jeremy_Bentham "Jeremy Bentham") was the founder of UCL, his
direct involvement was limited to the purchase of share No. 633, at a cost of
£100 paid in nine instalments between December 1826 and January 1830. In 1828,
he did nominate a friend to sit on the council, and in 1827, attempted to have
his disciple [John Bowring](/wiki/John_Bowring "John Bowring") appointed as
the first professor of English or History, but on both occasions his
candidates were unsuccessful.[23] However, Bentham is commonly regarded as the
"spiritual father" of UCL, as his ideas on education and society were
influential with the institution's founders, particularly [James
Mill](/wiki/James_Mill "James Mill") (1773–1836) and [Henry
Brougham](/wiki/Henry_Brougham,_1st_Baron_Brougham_and_Vaux "Henry Brougham,
1st Baron Brougham and Vaux") (1778–1868).[24]

In 1828, the chair of political economy at London University was created, with
[John Ramsay McCulloch](/wiki/John_Ramsay_McCulloch "John Ramsay McCulloch")
as the first incumbent.[25] In 1829, the university appointed the first
professor of English in England, although the course concentrated on
linguistics and the modern teaching of English – studying English literature –
was introduced by [King's College London](/wiki/King%27s_College_London
"King's College London") in 1831.[26] In 1830, London University founded the
London University School, which would later become [University College
School](/wiki/University_College_School "University College School").[27] In
1833, the university appointed [Alexander
Maconochie](/wiki/Alexander_Maconochie_\(penal_reformer\) "Alexander
Maconochie \(penal reformer\)"), secretary to the [Royal Geographical
Society](/wiki/Royal_Geographical_Society "Royal Geographical Society"), as
the first professor of geography in Britain.[28][29] Classes in medicine began
at the opening of the college in 1828, and in 1834 [University College
Hospital](/wiki/University_College_Hospital "University College Hospital")
(originally North London Hospital) opened as a teaching hospital for these
classes, which were organised into a faculty of medicine in 1836.[30]

### 1836 to 1900 – University College, London

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=University_College_London&action=edit&section=3
"Edit section: 1836 to 1900 – University College, London")]

After almost a decade of attempting to win recognition as a university and the
right to award degrees, including an Address to the Crown from the House of
Commons, the proprietors of London University accepted the government's
proposal to establish the University of London as an independent examining
body, accepting the status of a college for their institution.[31] As a
result, the proprietors of London University were incorporated by [royal
charter](/wiki/Royal_charter "Royal charter") under the name _University
College, London_ on 28 November 1836. On the same day, the [University of
London](/wiki/University_of_London "University of London") was created by
royal charter as a degree-awarding examining board for students from
affiliated schools and colleges, with University College and [King's
College](/wiki/King%27s_College_London "King's College London"), London being
named in the charter as the first two affiliates.[31][32] The first students
from UCL and King's matriculated as undergraduates in 1838 and the first
degrees were awarded to students of the two colleges in 1839.[33]

There had been an intention to establish a course in engineering at the
college's opening but no professor was appointed until 1840 or 1841, after
engineering courses had started at Durham University (1837) and King's College
London (1838).[34][35] The [Slade School of Fine
Art](/wiki/Slade_School_of_Fine_Art "Slade School of Fine Art") was founded as
part of University College in 1871, following a bequest from [Felix
Slade](/wiki/Felix_Slade "Felix Slade").[36]

In 1878, the University of London gained a supplemental charter making it the
first British university to be allowed to award degrees to women. The same
year, UCL admitted women to the faculties of Arts and Law and of Science,
although women remained barred from the faculties of Engineering and of
Medicine (with the exception of courses on public health and hygiene).[37][38]
UCL's admission of women in 1878 came almost three decades after [Bedford
College](/wiki/Bedford_College,_London "Bedford College, London") became the
first institution to offer university-level education for women in Britain,
and the establishment of the University of London's General Examination for
Women in 1868.[39][40]

The Ladies' Educational Association held classes for women from 1868, taught
by professors from UCL but independently of the college. From 1871 to 1872
these were held inside the college building, although still independently of
the college. From 1872, some professors, particularly [Edward
Poynter](/wiki/Edward_Poynter "Edward Poynter") of the Slade, started to admit
women to their classes.[41] The full opening on the faculties of arts, science
and law in 1878 came two years after the admission of women alongside men at
the [University of Bristol](/wiki/University_of_Bristol "University of
Bristol") from its foundation (as [University College
Bristol](/wiki/University_College_Bristol "University College Bristol")) in
1876.[42] The first woman to officially enrol in architecture at UCL was
[Gertrude Leverkus](/wiki/Gertrude_Leverkus "Gertrude Leverkus") in 1915,[43]
although [Ethel](/wiki/Ethel_Charles "Ethel Charles") and [Bessie
Charles](/wiki/Bessie_Charles "Bessie Charles") had been allowed to audit
classes in the 1890s.[44] Women were finally admitted to medical studies
during the First World War in 1917, although limitations were placed on their
numbers after the war ended.[45]

A new royal charter granted to the University of London in 1858 effectively
removed the affiliation of colleges to the university. Dissatisfaction from
the colleges and the desire for a "teaching university" in London led to royal
commissions that reported in 1888 and 1892 and the reconstitution of the
university under the University of London Act 1898.[31]

Following the University of London's reconstitution in 1909, transforming it
from an examining board to a federal university with constituent "schools",
UCL, became a school of the University of London. While most of the colleges
that became schools of the university retained their autonomy, UCL chose to be
merged into the university in 1907 under the University College London
(Transfer) Act 1905 ([5 Edw. 7](/wiki/5_Edw._7 "5 Edw. 7"). c. xci) and
surrendered its legal independence in return for gaining a greater say in the
running of the university.[31] Its formal name became _University of London,
University College_ , although for most informal and external purposes the
name "University College, London" (or the initialism UCL) was still used. As
of
2022,[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_College_London&action=edit)
it remains listed as "University of London: University College" on [US Federal
Student Aid](/wiki/FAFSA "FAFSA") applications.[46]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/37/The_Cruciform_Building_-
_geograph.org.uk_-_727084.jpg/250px-The_Cruciform_Building_-
_geograph.org.uk_-_727084.jpg)](/wiki/File:The_Cruciform_Building_-
_geograph.org.uk_-_727084.jpg)The Cruciform Building, seen from inside the
quadrangle of the UCL Main Building

1900 also saw the decision to appoint a salaried head of the college. The
first incumbent was [Carey Foster](/wiki/Carey_Foster "Carey Foster"), who
served as [Principal](/wiki/Principal_\(academia\) "Principal \(academia\)")
(as the post was originally titled) from 1900 to 1904. He was succeeded by
[Gregory Foster](/wiki/Gregory_Foster "Gregory Foster") (no relation), and in
1906 the title was changed to [Provost](/wiki/Provost_\(education\) "Provost
\(education\)") to avoid confusion with the principal of the University of
London. Gregory Foster remained in post until 1929.[47][48][49] In 1906, the
Cruciform Building was opened as the new home for [University College
Hospital](/wiki/University_College_Hospital "University College
Hospital").[50] UCL opened the [first department and chair of chemical
engineering](/wiki/Ramsay_Memorial_Professor_of_Chemical_Engineering "Ramsay
Memorial Professor of Chemical Engineering") in the UK, funded by the
[Ramsay](/wiki/William_Ramsay "William Ramsay") Memorial Fund, in 1923.[51]

In 1904, [Francis Galton](/wiki/Francis_Galton "Francis Galton") donated
£1,000 to the University of London for a [eugenics](/wiki/Eugenics "Eugenics")
laboratory; this transferred to UCL in 1907 with [Karl
Pearson](/wiki/Karl_Pearson "Karl Pearson") as its director.[52] UCL
apologised for its "fundamental role in the development, propagation and
legitimisation of eugenics" in 2021.[53]

In 1911, UCL received an anonymous donation of £30,000 (equivalent to
£3,860,000 in 2023) for a building for its [school of
architecture](/wiki/The_Bartlett "The Bartlett"). In 1919 the donor consented
to being named as [Herbert Bartlett](/wiki/Herbert_Bartlett "Herbert
Bartlett") and the school was renamed in his honour.[54]

UCL sustained considerable bomb damage during the Second World War, including
the complete destruction of the Great Hall, the Carey Foster Physics
Laboratory and the Ramsay Laboratory. Fires gutted the library and destroyed
much of the main building, including the dome; it was not until 1954 that the
main building was fully restored. The departments were dispersed across the
country to [Aberystwyth](/wiki/Aberystwyth "Aberystwyth"), [Bangor,
Gwynedd](/wiki/Bangor,_Gwynedd "Bangor, Gwynedd"), [Cambridge](/wiki/Cambridge
"Cambridge"), [Oxford](/wiki/Oxford "Oxford"),
[Rothamsted](/wiki/Rothamsted_Manor "Rothamsted Manor") near [Harpenden,
Hertfordshire](/wiki/Harpenden,_Hertfordshire "Harpenden, Hertfordshire") and
[Sheffield](/wiki/Sheffield "Sheffield"), with the administration at Stanstead
Bury near [Ware, Hertfordshire](/wiki/Ware,_Hertfordshire "Ware,
Hertfordshire").[55] The first UCL student newspaper,
_[Pi](/wiki/Pi_\(magazine\) "Pi \(magazine\)")_ , was founded in 1946.[56] The
[Institute of Jewish
Studies](/wiki/Institute_of_Jewish_Studies_at_University_College_London
"Institute of Jewish Studies at University College London") relocated from
Manchester to UCL in 1959.[57] The [Mullard Space Science
Laboratory](/wiki/Mullard_Space_Science_Laboratory "Mullard Space Science
Laboratory") was established in 1967.[58]

In 1973, [Peter Kirstein's](/wiki/Peter_T._Kirstein "Peter T. Kirstein")
research group at UCL became one of only two international nodes on the
[ARPANET](/wiki/ARPANET "ARPANET"), later becoming part of
[SATNET](/wiki/SATNET "SATNET").[59][60] UCL's implementation of
[internetworking](/wiki/Internetworking "Internetworking") between the ARPANET
and early [British academic
networks](/wiki/Internet_in_the_United_Kingdom#History "Internet in the United
Kingdom") was the first international heterogeneous [resource
sharing](/wiki/Resource_sharing "Resource sharing") network.[61] UCL played a
significant role in the very [earliest experimental Internet
work](/wiki/History_of_the_Internet "History of the Internet") and adopted
[TCP/IP](/wiki/TCP/IP "TCP/IP") in 1982, ahead of the
ARPANET.[62][63][64][note 1]

The college's [senior common room](/wiki/Common_room_\(university\) "Common
room \(university\)"), the Housman Room, remained men-only until 1969. After
two unsuccessful attempts, a motion was passed that ended segregation by sex
at UCL. This was achieved by [Brian Woledge](/wiki/Brian_Woledge "Brian
Woledge") (Fielden Professor of French at UCL from 1939 to 1971) and [David
Colquhoun](/wiki/David_Colquhoun "David Colquhoun"), at that time a young
lecturer in pharmacology.[65]

### 1976 to 2005 – University College London

In 1976, a new charter restored UCL's legal independence, although still
without the power to award its own degrees.[66][67] Under this charter the
college became formally known as _University College London_. This name
abandoned the comma used in its earlier name of _University College, London_.

In 1993, a reorganisation of the University of London meant that UCL and other
colleges gained direct access to government funding and the right to confer
University of London degrees themselves. This led to UCL being regarded as a
_de facto_ university in its own right.[68][69]

Mergers were a major feature of this period of UCL's history. In 1986, the
college merged with the [Institute of
Archaeology](/wiki/UCL_Institute_of_Archaeology "UCL Institute of
Archaeology").[70] In 1988, UCL merged with the Institute of Laryngology &
Otology, the Institute of Orthopaedics, the Institute of Urology & Nephrology
and [Middlesex Hospital Medical School](/wiki/Middlesex_Hospital "Middlesex
Hospital").[70] Middlesex and University College hospitals, together with the
Elizabeth Garrett Anderson Hospital and the Hospital for Tropical Diseases,
formed the [University College London Hospitals NHS
Trust](/wiki/University_College_London_Hospitals_NHS_Foundation_Trust
"University College London Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust") in 1994.[71]

Mergers continued in the 1990s, with the [Institute of Child
Health](/wiki/UCL_Institute_of_Child_Health "UCL Institute of Child Health")
joining in 1995, the School of Podiatry in 1996[72] and the [Institute of
Neurology](/wiki/UCL_Institute_of_Neurology "UCL Institute of Neurology") in
1997.[70][73] In 1998, UCL merged with the Royal Free Hospital Medical School
to create the Royal Free and University College Medical School (renamed the
[UCL Medical School](/wiki/UCL_Medical_School "UCL Medical School") in October
2008). In 1999, UCL merged with the [School of Slavonic and East European
Studies](/wiki/UCL_School_of_Slavonic_and_East_European_Studies "UCL School of
Slavonic and East European Studies")[74][75] and the [Eastman Dental
Institute](/wiki/UCL_Eastman_Dental_Institute "UCL Eastman Dental
Institute").[70]

Proposals for a merger between UCL and [Imperial College
London](/wiki/Imperial_College_London "Imperial College London") were
announced in 2002.[76] The proposal provoked strong opposition from UCL
teaching staff and students and the [AUT
union](/wiki/Association_of_University_Teachers "Association of University
Teachers"), which criticised "the indecent haste and lack of consultation",
leading to its abandonment by UCL provost Sir [Derek
Roberts](/wiki/Derek_Roberts "Derek Roberts").[77][78]

### From 2005

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=University_College_London&action=edit&section=6
"Edit section: From 2005")]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/dc/The_UCL_School_of_Slavonic_and_East_European_Studies.jpg/250px-
The_UCL_School_of_Slavonic_and_East_European_Studies.jpg)](/wiki/File:The_UCL_School_of_Slavonic_and_East_European_Studies.jpg)The
[UCL School of Slavonic and East European
Studies](/wiki/UCL_School_of_Slavonic_and_East_European_Studies "UCL School of
Slavonic and East European Studies") building, which was opened in 2005

UCL was granted its own taught and research degree awarding powers in
2005,[79] and all UCL students registered from 2007/08 qualified with UCL
degrees.[80] The same year, UCL adopted a new corporate branding under which
the name University College London was replaced by the
[initialism](/wiki/Acronym_and_initialism "Acronym and initialism") UCL in all
external communications.[81]

UCL established the UCL School of Energy & Resources (later [UCL
Australia](/wiki/UCL_Australia "UCL Australia")) in [Adelaide](/wiki/Adelaide
"Adelaide"), Australia, in 2008 as the first campus of a British university in
the country.[82] The school was based in the historic [Torrens
Building](/wiki/Torrens_Building "Torrens Building") in Victoria Square.[83]
In 2011, the mining company [BHP Billiton](/wiki/BHP "BHP") agreed to donate
AU$10 million to UCL to fund the establishment of two energy institutes – the
Energy Policy Institute, based in Adelaide, and the Institute for Sustainable
Resources, based in London.[84] UCL Australia closed in December 2017, with
academic staff and student transferring to the [University of South
Australia](/wiki/University_of_South_Australia "University of South
Australia").[85] Since 2018, UCL and the University of South Australia have
offered joint master's degrees in data science and in energy systems with
study in Adelaide and London.[86]

In 2011, UCL announced plans for a £500 million investment in its main
Bloomsbury campus over 10 years, as well as the establishment of a new campus,
[UCL East](/wiki/UCL_East "UCL East"), next to the Olympic Park in Stratford
in the East End of London.[87] In 2018, UCL opened _UCL at Here East_ , at the
Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park, offering courses jointly between the [Bartlett
Faculty of the Built Environment](/wiki/The_Bartlett "The Bartlett") and the
[Faculty of Engineering Sciences](/wiki/UCL_Faculty_of_Engineering_Sciences
"UCL Faculty of Engineering Sciences").[88][89] The first undergraduate
students, on a new Engineering and Architectural Design [MEng](/wiki/MEng
"MEng"), started in September 2018.[90] One Pool Street, the first building on
the UCL East campus, opened in November 2022. UCL East was officially opened,
along with the Marshgate building that completed phase 1 of the development,
in September 2023 by Olympic gold medalist and UCL alumna [Christine
Ohuruogu](/wiki/Christine_Ohuruogu "Christine Ohuruogu").[91][92]

UCL continued to grow through mergers with smaller colleges in the University
of London. On 1 January 2012 the [School of Pharmacy, University of
London](/wiki/School_of_Pharmacy,_University_of_London "School of Pharmacy,
University of London") merged with UCL, becoming the UCL School of Pharmacy
within the Faculty of Life Sciences.[93][94] UCL and the [Institute of
Education](/wiki/Institute_of_Education "Institute of Education") formed a
strategic alliance in October 2012,[95] followed by a full merger in December
2014.[96][97][98][99]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0b/Student_Centre_in_the_afternoon%2C_University_College_London.jpg/250px-
Student_Centre_in_the_afternoon%2C_University_College_London.jpg)](/wiki/File:Student_Centre_in_the_afternoon,_University_College_London.jpg)New
Student Centre on [Gordon Street](/wiki/Gordon_Street "Gordon Street")

UCL paid tens of thousands of pounds to settle ten sexual harassment claims
against staff in the 2017/18 academic year, a rise from four cases the year
before. Following pressure from victims, and after physicist [Emma
Chapman](/wiki/Emma_Chapman "Emma Chapman") won the legal right to speak
freely about her abuse at the university, UCL announced in 2018 that it would
abandon non-disclosure settlements in settlements.[100][101] In 2020, UCL
became the first [Russell Group](/wiki/Russell_Group "Russell Group")
university to ban romantic and sexual relationships between lecturers and
their students.[102]

It was discovered in 2018 that an annual eugenics conference, the [London
Conference on Intelligence](/wiki/London_Conference_on_Intelligence "London
Conference on Intelligence"), had been held at UCL, as an external paid event,
between 2014 and 2017.[103] An enquiry found that the organiser, an honorary
lecturer, did not correctly follow the room booking procedure, including
claiming that no controversial topics would be discussed, leaving the
university unaware of the nature of the conference.[104] Following the
revelation, UCL announced in 2018 that it would launch an enquiry into the
university's historical links with eugenics.[105] This reported in 2020,[106]
but covered only historical eugenics and did not address the 2014–17
conferences, leading to a majority of the authors refusing to sign the final
report.[107] The Galton Lecture Theatre, Pearson Lecture Theatre and Pearson
Building were all renamed in 2020,[107] and in 2021 UCL apologised for its
part in promoting [eugenics](/wiki/Eugenics "Eugenics") during the first half
of the 20th century.[53][108] UCL was criticised (along with Oxford, Imperial
and other London universities) in 2021 for accepting money from the Alexander
Mosley Charitable Trust, established to hold the fortune left to [Max
Mosley](/wiki/Max_Mosley "Max Mosley") by his father, British fascist leader
[Oswald Mosley](/wiki/Oswald_Mosley "Oswald Mosley"). UCL received £500,000 to
establish a forensic evidence interpretation laboratory.[109][110][111]

Following the passing of the University of London Act 2018, which allowed
member institutions to become universities in their own right while remaining
part of the University of London, UCL applied for university status in
2019.[112] The application was approved by the [Office for
Students](/wiki/Office_for_Students "Office for Students") in 2022 and a
supplemental charter was sealed on 17 April 2023, granting UCL university
status.[113]

UCL is primarily based in the [Bloomsbury](/wiki/Bloomsbury "Bloomsbury") area
of the [London Borough of Camden](/wiki/London_Borough_of_Camden "London
Borough of Camden"), in [Central London](/wiki/Central_London "Central

other departments close by in Bloomsbury.[114] Many health institutes are
located close to associated hospitals, including the [UCL Queen Square
Institute of Neurology](/wiki/UCL_Queen_Square_Institute_of_Neurology "UCL
Queen Square Institute of Neurology") and the [National Hospital for Neurology
and Neurosurgery](/wiki/National_Hospital_for_Neurology_and_Neurosurgery
"National Hospital for Neurology and Neurosurgery") in [Queen
Square](/wiki/Queen_Square,_London "Queen Square, London"),[115] the [UCL
Great Ormond Street Institute of Child
Health](/wiki/UCL_Great_Ormond_Street_Institute_of_Child_Health "UCL Great

London](/wiki/Halls_of_residence_at_University_College_London "Halls of
residence at University College London")

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/bf/Unbridled_facadism%2C_Caledonian_Road%2C_N7_%28geograph_5265516%29.jpg/250px-
Unbridled_facadism%2C_Caledonian_Road%2C_N7_%28geograph_5265516%29.jpg)](/wiki/File:Unbridled_facadism,_Caledonian_Road,_N7_\(geograph_5265516\).jpg)The

UCL owns 26 halls of residence with around 7,000 student beds.[134] The
university guarantees accommodation to single full-time first-year
undergraduate students who have not previously lived in London while studying
at a university, and who make a firm acceptance of a place and apply for
accommodation by 10 June each year, and to single overseas first-year
postgraduates at UCL who have not previously lived in London while studying at
a university, and who make a firm acceptance of a place and apply for
accommodation by 30 June each year. Accommodation is also guaranteed for
students who are under 18 at the start of the academic year and for students
who are care-leavers.[135] There is only limited accommodation available in
university halls for returning students and others who do not meet the
criteria for a guaranteed place.[136] UCL students are also eligible, as
students of a member institution of the University of London, to apply for
places in the [University of London intercollegiate halls of
residence](/wiki/University_of_London#Student_housing "University of
London").[137]

In 2013, UCL's newly built New Hall student accommodation building on
[Caledonian Road](/wiki/Caledonian_Road,_London "Caledonian Road, London"),
designed by Stephen George and Partners, was awarded the [Carbuncle
Cup](/wiki/Carbuncle_Cup "Carbuncle Cup") and named the country's worst new
building by _[Building Design](/wiki/Building_Design "Building Design")_
magazine, with the comment "this is a building that the jury struggled to see
as remotely fit for human occupation". Islington Council had originally turned
down planning permission for the building, but this had been overturned on
appeal. As it is classified as a hotel or guest house, it was exempt from many
of the standards that cover residential buildings, such as having daylight in
the rooms.[138][139]

The UCL East development includes 532 student rooms in One Pool Street, which
opened in 2022.[140] Further accommodation will be available in the Marshgate
building, expected to open in 2023, and at the second Pool Street site.[141]

### Environmental initiatives

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=University_College_London&action=edit&section=12
"Edit section: Environmental initiatives")]

UCL's new Student Centre, which opened in 2019, was designed to be
environmentally friendly and was one of only 320 buildings worldwide (at the
time) to be certified _outstanding_ by [BREEAM](/wiki/BREEAM "BREEAM").[142]
This certification requires innovation throughout the design, engineering and
construction process, and places the Student Centre among the top 1% of non-
domestic buildings in the UK for sustainability.[143] The UCL Student Centre
was a finalist at the [Green Gown Awards](/wiki/Green_Gown_Awards "Green Gown
Awards") in 2019.[144]

Also in 2019, UCL launched a _Strategy for Sustainable UCL 2019–24_ ,
including three initiatives to promote sustainability. The _Positive Climate_
initiative saw UCL pledge to have a 40% reduction in energy usage, all energy
to come from renewables, and all UCL buildings to be [carbon
neutral](/wiki/Carbon_neutral "Carbon neutral") by 2024, along with achieving
[net zero](/wiki/Net_zero "Net zero") carbon emissions for UCL by 2030.[142]
The _Positive Climate_ initiative was the winner in the "2030 Climate Action"
category at the 2020 Green Gown Awards.[145][146]

A second initiative, _The Loop_ , promotes [circular
economy](/wiki/Circular_economy "Circular economy"). UCL set a target of
reducing waste per person by 20% between 2019 and 2024, while aiming for an
85% recycling rate and the elimination of single-use plastics on campus. The
third initiative, _Wild Bloomsbury_ , promotes
[biodiversity](/wiki/Biodiversity "Biodiversity"). UCL set a target of
creating 10,000 m2 (1.0 ha; 2.5 acres) of biodiverse green space on campus by
2024.[142] The _Strategy for a Sustainable UCL_ was a finalist in the
"Sustainable Institution of the Year" category at the 2022 Green Gown
Awards.[147]

UCL was ranked joint fifth globally for sustainability in the _[QS World
University Rankings](/wiki/QS_World_University_Rankings "QS World University
Rankings"): Sustainability 2025_.[148] In the national _[People and
Planet](/wiki/People_and_Planet "People and Planet") University League_ for
2023/24, it was ranked 12th (1st class).[149]

### Governance

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=University_College_London&action=edit&section=14
"Edit section: Governance")]

The two main bodies in UCL's governance structure are the
[council](/wiki/University_council "University council") and the [academic
board](/wiki/Academic_senate "Academic senate"), both of which are established
by the royal charter and with powers defined by the statutes.[150] There is
also a University Management Committee, which is the executive committee
responsible for the day-to-day operations of the institution. This comprises
the President and Provost, the vice-presidents, the vice-provosts, the pro-
provost of UCL East, the deans of the faculties, the chief financial officer,
chief information officer, and chief people officer, the chief of staff, the
general consul, the executive director of media and marketing, and the
director of media relations.[151]

The senior leadership team at UCL includes the [visitor](/wiki/Visitor
"Visitor"), a position in English charity law that oversees the operation of
the institution.[152] That there shall be a visitor of the college is
specified by the royal charter, as is that the position is to be held by the
[Master of the Rolls](/wiki/Master_of_the_Rolls "Master of the Rolls"), the
second most senior judge in England and Wales.[150]

UCL's council comprises 20 members, of whom 11 are members external to UCL;
seven are UCL academic staff, including the provost, three UCL professors and
three non-professorial staff; and two are UCL students. The chair is appointed
by council for a term not normally exceeding five years. The chair is _ex
officio_ chair of the honorary degrees and fellowships committee, nominations
committee and remuneration and strategy committee.[153] As of April
2023,[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_College_London&action=edit)
the chair of the council is international businessman and UCL alumnus Victor
Chu.[4]

The academic board plays a role similar to the [senate](/wiki/Academic_senate
"Academic senate") in other institutions. It is the senior academic body
responsible for advising council on academic matters and also elects academic
members to council. It is, however, a much larger body than the senates at
many other universities, including all professors as well as elected
representatives of other academic and non-academic staff.[150][154]

UCL's principal academic and administrative officer is the President and
Provost, who is also UCL's designated _[accountable
officer](/wiki/Office_for_Students#Accountable_officer "Office for Students")_
for reporting to the [Office for Students](/wiki/Office_for_Students "Office
for Students") on behalf of UCL.[155] The provost is appointed by Council
after consultation with the academic board, and is _ex officio_ a member of
council and chair of the academic board.[156] [Michael
Spence](/wiki/Michael_Spence_\(legal_scholar\) "Michael Spence \(legal
scholar\)") has been president and provost since January 2021, when he
succeeded [Michael Arthur](/wiki/Michael_Arthur_\(physician\) "Michael Arthur
\(physician\)").[157][158]

Vice-provosts are appointed by council on the recommendation of the provost or
the academic board, to assist and advise the provost as required. The vice-
provosts are members of the provost's senior management team. There are four
vice-provosts (for education and student experience; health; research,
innovation and global engagement; and faculties).[150][159] There are also
four vice-presidents, who are also members of the senior management team but
whose role and manner of appointment is not specified in the statutes, for
strategy, external engagement, advancement and operations.[150][159]

The deans of UCL's faculties are appointed by the council and are members of
the provost's senior management team. The deans' principal duties include
advising the provost and vice-provosts on academic strategy, staffing matters
and resources for academic departments within their faculty; overseeing
curricula and programme management at faculty level; liaising with faculty
tutors on undergraduate admissions and student academic matters; overseeing
examination matters at faculty level; and co-ordinating faculty views on
matters relating to education and information support.[153]

### Finances

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=University_College_London&action=edit&section=16
"Edit section: Finances")]

In the financial year ended 31 July 2024, UCL had a total income (excluding
share of joint ventures) of £2.03 billion (2022/23 – £1.93 billion) and a
total expenditure of £1.47 billion (2022/23 – £1.71 billion).[2] Key sources
of income included £538.8 million from research grants and contracts (2022/23
– £526.7 million), £971.2 million from tuition fees and education contracts
(2022/23 – £929.3 million), £228.1 million from funding body grants (2022/23 –
£236.7 million) and £34.1 million from donations and endowments (2022/23 –
£31.5 million).[2] At year end UCL had endowments of £174.8 million (31 July
2023 – £156.8 million) and total net assets of £2.19 billion (31 July 2023 –
£1.61 million).[2]

A report by London Economics in 2022 found that UCL generates around £10
billion annually for the UK economy. The largest contributor to this is
through the spread of its research and knowledge, which is worth £4 billion,
with another £3 billion being added by the impact of UCL's own spending. Other
contributions come from encouraging graduates to create jobs and investment,
and from nurturing company spin-offs and start-ups. The report found that in
2018–19, UCL had supported 234 graduate start-ups and 83 spinout companies,
with a total turnover of £110 million and employing almost 3,000 people. The
report also found that UCL's spending supported 19,000 jobs across the UK,
with over 7,000 of these being outside London.[13]

### Terms

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=University_College_London&action=edit&section=17
"Edit section: Terms")]

The UCL academic year is divided into three terms. For most departments, First
Term runs from late September to mid-December, Second Term from mid-January to
late March, and Third Term from late April to mid-June, with reading weeks in
early November and mid-February. Certain courses at the medical school, the
faculty of education and society, and the school of pharmacy operate on
different terms.[164]

### Logo and colours

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=University_College_London&action=edit&section=18
"Edit section: Logo and colours")]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/5/58/UCL_old_logo.jpg/250px-
UCL_old_logo.jpg)](/wiki/File:UCL_old_logo.jpg)The old UCL logo, used prior to
August 2005

While many universities use their logo for most communications and branding
and a coat of arms only for specific ceremonial and official use,[165] UCL
exclusively uses a logo and has no coat of arms. The present logo was adopted
as part of a rebranding exercise in August 2005.[81] Prior to that date, a
different logo was used, in which the letters UCL were incorporated into a
stylised representation of the Wilkins Building [portico](/wiki/Portico
"Portico").[166]

A pseudo-heraldic "UCL crest" – a purple shield depicting a raised bent arm
dressed in armour between two gold laurel branches holding a green upturned
open wreath, with the college motto on a blue celeste ribbon beneath the
laurel branches – can be found on the internet. A version of this badge (not
on a shield) appears to have been used by [UCL
Union](/wiki/University_College_London_Union "University College London
Union") from shortly after its foundation in 1893.[167] However, the badge has
never been the subject of an official [grant of arms](/wiki/Grant_of_arms
"Grant of arms"), and departs from several of the rules and conventions of
[heraldry](/wiki/Heraldry "Heraldry"). It is not an official logo, although
modified forms are used by some by sports teams and societies.[168] The
official Team UCL logo, used (with variants) by many sports teams, uses a
shield divided into the colours of purple (lower) and blue celeste (upper),
but none of the other elements (laurels, wreaths, armoured arm, motto) are
present; the only graphic is a depiction of the UCL portico. Students' Union
UCL requests teams not to modify this logo, but this is widely
ignored.[169][170]

UCL's motto, "_Cuncti adsint meritaeque expectent praemia palmae_ " is a
quotation from [Virgil](/wiki/Virgil "Virgil")'s _[Aeneid](/wiki/Aeneid
"Aeneid")_ , and translates into English as "Let all come who by merit deserve
the most reward".[171][172]

UCL's traditional sporting and academic colours are purple and blue
celeste.[7] UCL uses a palette of 25 colours (including the two traditional
colours) in its visual identity; the logo can be used in many different
combinations of these colours.[7]

### Memberships, affiliations and partnerships

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=University_College_London&action=edit&section=19
"Edit section: Memberships, affiliations and partnerships")]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b5/University_College_Hospital_-
_New_Building_-_London_-_020504.jpg/250px-University_College_Hospital_-
_New_Building_-_London_-_020504.jpg)](/wiki/File:University_College_Hospital_-
_New_Building_-_London_-_020504.jpg)The main building of [University College
Hospital](/wiki/University_College_Hospital "University College Hospital")

UCL is a member institution of the federal University of London and was one of
the two colleges affiliated from the university's founding in 1836 (the other
being [King's College London](/wiki/King%27s_College_London "King's College
London")).[173] UCL was a founding member of the [Russell
Group](/wiki/Russell_Group "Russell Group"), an association of 24 British
research universities established in 1994,[174] and is regarded as forming
part of the '[golden triangle](/wiki/Golden_triangle_\(universities\) "Golden
triangle \(universities\)")', an unofficial term for the research-intensive
universities located in the southern English cities of Cambridge, London and
Oxford[175][176][177]

UCL has been a member of the [League of European Research
Universities](/wiki/League_of_European_Research_Universities "League of
European Research Universities") since January 2006.[178][179] UCL is also a
member of the [Association of Commonwealth
Universities](/wiki/Association_of_Commonwealth_Universities "Association of
Commonwealth Universities"),[180] the [European University
Association](/wiki/European_University_Association "European University
Association"),[181] the global U7+ Alliance[182] and the US [Universities
Research Association](/wiki/Universities_Research_Association "Universities
Research Association"),[183] and has a major collaboration with [Yale
University](/wiki/Yale_University "Yale University"), the Yale UCL
Collaborative.[184] It also has partnerships with universities in
Australia,[note 2] Canada,[note 3] China,[note 4] India,[note 5] Japan,[note
6] Singapore[note 7] and Thailand.[note 8][185][186][187][188]

UCL formed the [Science and Engineering
South](/wiki/Science_and_Engineering_South "Science and Engineering South")
engineering and physical sciences research alliance with the universities of
Cambridge, Oxford, Southampton and Imperial College London in May 2013.[189]
It was also one of the founding members of the [Alan Turing
Institute](/wiki/Alan_Turing_Institute "Alan Turing Institute"), the UK's
national institute for data sciences and artificial intelligence, in 2015,
with the universities of Cambridge, Edinburgh, Oxford and Warwick.[190]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/15/Francis_Crick_Institute_building%2C_Oct_2015.jpg/250px-
Francis_Crick_Institute_building%2C_Oct_2015.jpg)](/wiki/File:Francis_Crick_Institute_building,_Oct_2015.jpg)The
[Francis Crick Institute](/wiki/Francis_Crick_Institute "Francis Crick
Institute") building

UCL is a partner in [UCLPartners](/wiki/UCLPartners "UCLPartners"), an
[academic health science centre](/wiki/Academic_medical_centre "Academic
medical centre"), along with multiple NHS trusts, integrated care systems,
research and innovation partners, and other universities.[191] UCL is a
partner with the [National Institute for Health
Research](/wiki/National_Institute_for_Health_Research "National Institute for
Health Research"), the [University College London Hospitals NHS Foundation

### Research

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=University_College_London&action=edit&section=21
"Edit section: Research")]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/ab/John_O%27Keefe_%28neuroscientist%29_2014.jpg/250px-
John_O%27Keefe_%28neuroscientist%29_2014.jpg)](/wiki/File:John_O%27Keefe_\(neuroscientist\)_2014.jpg)[John
O'Keefe](/wiki/John_O%27Keefe_\(neuroscientist\) "John O'Keefe
\(neuroscientist\)"), UCL neuroscientist and 2014 Nobel laureate for his
discovery of [place cells](/wiki/Place_cell "Place cell")

In 2023/24, UCL had an income from research grants and contracts of £538.8
million, making up 26.6% of all revenue. The largest sources of research
income were research council grants (£175.9 million) and British charities
(£154.2 million). A further £164 million of recurrent research funding was
allocated to UCL by [Research England](/wiki/Research_England "Research
England"), making up 8% of income.[2]

UCL submitted 3,432 staff (3,177 FTEs) across 32 units of assessment (areas of
research) to the 2021 [Research Excellence
Framework](/wiki/Research_Excellence_Framework "Research Excellence
Framework") (REF) assessment. 58% of submitted research was rated 4* ('world
leading'), the sixth highest in the REF, and a further 34% as 3*
('internationally excellent'). Overall, UCL was ranked second for both
research power and market share by both _Times Higher Education_ and _Research
Professional News_ , and sixth on research quality (GPA) by _Times Higher
Education_. UCL submitted more units of assessment to the 2021 REF than any
other university. However, UCL's market share (based on the funding formula)
declined from 6.23% following the 2014 REF to 5.34%, despite the overall
improvement, reflecting increases in research quality across the
sector.[201][202][203][204]

#### Research centres

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=University_College_London&action=edit&section=22
"Edit section: Research centres")]

UCL operates a large number of disciplinary-specific research centres in
partnership with other research institutions and private enterprises. Notable
examples include:

  * The [London Centre for Nanotechnology](/wiki/London_Centre_for_Nanotechnology "London Centre for Nanotechnology") (LCN), a multidisciplinary research centre in physical and biomedical nanotechnology based at UCL's campus in Bloomsbury. It is a partnership between UCL, [Imperial College London](/wiki/Imperial_College_London "Imperial College London") and [King's College London](/wiki/King%27s_College_London "King's College London").[205] The LCN was established as a joint venture between UCL and Imperial College London in 2003;[206] King's College London joined the LCN in 2018.[207]
  * The [Centre for the Study of the Legacies of British Slave-ownership](/wiki/Centre_for_the_Study_of_the_Legacies_of_British_Slave-ownership "Centre for the Study of the Legacies of British Slave-ownership"), which was established at UCL with the support of the [Hutchins Center for African and African American Research](/wiki/Hutchins_Center_for_African_and_African_American_Research "Hutchins Center for African and African American Research") at [Harvard University](/wiki/Harvard_University "Harvard University"). It incorporates two earlier projects: the _Legacies of British Slave-ownership project_ (2009–2012) and the _Structure and significance of British Caribbean slave-ownership_ 1763–1833 project (2013–2015).[208]
  * The [Sainsbury Wellcome Centre for Neural Circuits and Behaviour](/wiki/Sainsbury_Wellcome_Centre_for_Neural_Circuits_and_Behaviour "Sainsbury Wellcome Centre for Neural Circuits and Behaviour") (SWC), a neuroscience research centre established at UCL with funding from the [Gatsby Charitable Foundation](/wiki/Gatsby_Charitable_Foundation "Gatsby Charitable Foundation") and [Wellcome Trust](/wiki/Wellcome_Trust "Wellcome Trust") and opened in 2016.[209][210]

#### Publishing and commercialisation

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=University_College_London&action=edit&section=23
"Edit section: Publishing and commercialisation")]

In 2020/21, UCL had an income of £7.3 million from intellectual property and
£25.2 million from the sale of shares in spin-off companies. As of 2020/21,
UCL had the second largest patent portfolio of any UK university (after
Oxford) with 2,391 patents. It granted the third largest number of
intellectual property licences (after Oxford and the University of East
Anglia), with 2,235.[211]

[UCL Business](/wiki/UCL_Business "UCL Business") is a [technology
transfer](/wiki/Technology_transfer "Technology transfer") company which is
wholly owned by UCL. It has three main activities: licensing technologies,
creating spin-out companies, and project management.[212] UCL Business
supports spin-out companies in areas including discovery disclosure,
commercialisation, business plan development, contractual advice, incubation
support, recruitment of management teams and identification of investors.[212]
In the area of licensing technoloiges, the company provides commercial, legal
and administrative advice to help companies broker licensing agreements.[212]
UCL Business also provides UCL departments and institutes with project
management services for single or multi-party collaborative industry
projects.[212] The company transferred £11 million of royalty income to UCL in
2023/24 (2022/23: £3.1 million).[2]

Launched in 2015, UCL Press is a [new university
press](/wiki/University_press#NUP "University press")[213] wholly owned by
UCL.[214] It was the first fully [open access](/wiki/Open_access "Open
access") university press in the UK, and publishes monographs, textbooks and
other academic books in a wide range of academic areas which are available to
download for free, in addition to a number of journals.[215] As of December
2024, UCL Press had had more than 13 million downloads of its open access
books and journal articles in 242 countries and territories worldwide. More
than 10 million of these were for its open access books.[216] UCL Consultants
is an academic consultancy services company which is wholly owned by UCL,
which provides four main service offerings: Academic Consultancy, Bespoke
Short Courses, Testing & Analysis and Expert Witness.[217][218]

### Libraries

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=University_College_London&action=edit&section=24
"Edit section: Libraries")]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/dd/Donaldson_Reading_Room%2C_UCL.jpg/250px-
Donaldson_Reading_Room%2C_UCL.jpg)](/wiki/File:Donaldson_Reading_Room,_UCL.jpg)The

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/63/IOE_Newsam_Library.JPG/250px-

The UCL library system comprises 18 libraries located across the Bloomsbury
and UCL East campuses.[219] The libraries contain a total of over 2 million
books.[220] The largest library is the UCL Main Library, which is located in
the UCL Main Building and contains collections relating to the arts and
humanities, economics, history, law and public policy.[219] The second largest
library is the UCL Science Library, which is located in the DMS Watson
Building on Malet Place and contains collections relating to anthropology,
engineering, geography, life sciences, management and the mathematical and
physical sciences.[219] The Cruciform Hub contains books and periodicals in
the subjects of clinical medicine and medical science.[221] It holds the
combined collections of the former Boldero and Clinical Sciences libraries
which developed within the [Middlesex Hospital](/wiki/Middlesex_Hospital
"Middlesex Hospital"), [University College
Hospital](/wiki/University_College_Hospital "University College Hospital") and
[Royal Free](/wiki/Royal_Free_Hospital "Royal Free Hospital") & [University
College Medical Schools](/wiki/UCL_Medical_School "UCL Medical School") up
until their merger in 2005.[222]

Other libraries include the [UCL Bartlett](/wiki/The_Bartlett "The Bartlett")
Library (architecture and town planning), the [UCL Eastman Dental Institute
Library](/wiki/UCL_Eastman_Dental_Institute#Library "UCL Eastman Dental
Institute") (oral health sciences), the [UCL Institute of
Archaeology](/wiki/UCL_Institute_of_Archaeology "UCL Institute of
Archaeology") Library (archaeology and egyptology), the UCL Institute of
Education's [Newsam Library](/wiki/Institute_of_Education#Library "Institute
of Education") (education and related areas of social science), the [UCL
Institute of Neurology Rockefeller Medical
Library](/wiki/UCL_Institute_of_Neurology#Library "UCL Institute of
Neurology") (neurosurgery and neuroscience), the [Joint Moorfields Eye
Hospital & the UCL Institute of Ophthalmology
Library](/wiki/UCL_Institute_of_Ophthalmology#Library "UCL Institute of
Ophthalmology") (biomedicine, medicine, nursing, ophthalmology and visual
science), the UCL Language & Speech Science Library (audiology, communication
disorders, linguistics & phonetics, special education, speech & language
therapy and voice) and the [UCL School of Slavonic and East European Studies
Library](/wiki/UCL_School_of_Slavonic_and_East_European_Studies#Library "UCL
School of Slavonic and East European Studies") (the economics, geography,
history, languages, literature and politics of Eastern Europe).[219] The
newest library is the UCL East Library, currently located in the Learning Hub
on the first floor of One Pool Street. Uniquely among UCL libraries, it offers
a 'click and collect' service allowing books from any UCL library to be
delivered to UCL East rather than having to be picked up from the library that
holds them. It is expected to relocate to the new Marshgate building when that
opens in September 2023.[223]

UCL staff and students have full access to the main libraries of the
University of London – the [Senate House Library](/wiki/Senate_House_Library
"Senate House Library") and the libraries of the institutes of the [School of
Advanced Study](/wiki/School_of_Advanced_Study "School of Advanced Study") –
which are located close to the main UCL campus in Bloomsbury.[224] These
libraries contain over 3.7 million books and focus on the arts, humanities and
social sciences.[220] The [British Library](/wiki/British_Library "British
Library"), which contains around 14 million books, is also located close to
the main UCL campus and all UCL students and staff can apply for reference
access.[225]

UCL's [open access](/wiki/Open_access "Open access") [institutional
repository](/wiki/Institutional_repository "Institutional repository"), UCL
Discovery, and [UCL Press](/wiki/UCL_Press "UCL Press"), UCL's open access
[academic press](/wiki/University_press "University press") are managed by UCL
Library Services.[226]

#### Special collections

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=University_College_London&action=edit&section=25
"Edit section: Special collections")]

UCL's Special Collections contains UCL's collection of historical or
culturally significant works. It holds over 150,000 rare books, including 179
[incunabula](/wiki/Incunabula "Incunabula"), as well as over 600 collections
of archives and manuscripts. The incunabula include a 1477 edition of Dante's
_[Divine Comedy](/wiki/Divine_Comedy "Divine Comedy")_ , and a 1493 edition of
the _[Nuremberg Chronicle](/wiki/Nuremberg_Chronicle "Nuremberg Chronicle")_
donated by Jeremy Bentham.[227][228]

UCL's most significant works are housed in three strong rooms. The special
collection includes first editions of [Isaac Newton](/wiki/Isaac_Newton "Isaac
Newton")'s _[Principia](/wiki/Philosophiae_Naturalis_Principia_Mathematica
"Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica")_ , [Charles
Darwin](/wiki/Charles_Darwin "Charles Darwin")'s _[On the Origin of
Species](/wiki/On_the_Origin_of_Species "On the Origin of Species")_ and
[James Joyce](/wiki/James_Joyce "James Joyce")'s
_[Ulysses](/wiki/Ulysses_\(novel\) "Ulysses \(novel\)")_.[229]

### Museums

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=University_College_London&action=edit&section=26
"Edit section: Museums")]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/20/Flaxman_Gallery%2C_UCL.JPG/250px-
Flaxman_Gallery%2C_UCL.JPG)](/wiki/File:Flaxman_Gallery,_UCL.JPG)The Flaxman
Gallery

UCL is responsible for several museums and collections in a wide range of
fields across the arts and sciences, including:[230]

  * [Petrie Museum of Egyptian Archaeology](/wiki/Petrie_Museum_of_Egyptian_Archaeology "Petrie Museum of Egyptian Archaeology"): Founded in 1892 by a donation from [Amelia Edwards](/wiki/Amelia_Edwards "Amelia Edwards") of several hundred Egyptian items, the museum now contains around 80,000 items and covers the history of the Nile valley from prehistoric times through to the Islamic period. It is named after [William Flinders Petrie](/wiki/William_Flinders_Petrie "William Flinders Petrie"), the first Edwards Professor at UCL, who excavated dozens of sites in his career and sold his collection to the college in 1913.[231] The Petrie Museum is a _[designated collection](/wiki/Designation_Scheme "Designation Scheme")_ under the [Arts Council England](/wiki/Arts_Council_England "Arts Council England") Designation Scheme for "pre-eminent collections held in museums, libraries and archives across England".[232]
  * UCL Art Museum: the art collection originated as a teaching and research collection for the Slade, and contains works by women artists dating back to the 1890s. A series of plaster casts of full-size details of sculptures by [John Flaxman](/wiki/John_Flaxman "John Flaxman") is located inside the library under the dome of the UCL Main Building.[233] It was announced in 2024 that this would be closed to allow the area to become a flexible event space, with the objects placed in storage until a new gallery could be provided elsewhere.[234]
  * [Grant Museum of Zoology and Comparative Anatomy](/wiki/Grant_Museum_of_Zoology_and_Comparative_Anatomy "Grant Museum of Zoology and Comparative Anatomy"): Established in 1827 by [Robert Edmund Grant](/wiki/Robert_Edmund_Grant "Robert Edmund Grant"), UCL's first professor of comparative anatomy and zoology, for teaching purposes. Grant bequeathed his collection of 10,000 specimens to UCL upon his death. With other additions, the museum now contains around 68,000 specimens, including [dodo](/wiki/Dodo "Dodo") bones and a rare [quagga](/wiki/Quagga "Quagga") skeleton.[235]

National

UCL is ranked as one of the top fifteen universities in all three of the main
[UK university league
tables](/wiki/Rankings_of_universities_in_the_United_Kingdom "Rankings of
universities in the United Kingdom").[236][237][238] These place more emphasis
on teaching and student experience than global rankings, using criteria such
as teaching quality and learning resources, entry standards, employment
prospects, research quality and dropout rates.[242] It went through a dip in
rankings in the mid 2010s, particularly in _The Guardian University Guide_ ,
but returned to that publication's top ten in the 2022 rankings, when its
ninth position was its best result since 2014.[243]

In the 2023 _Complete University Guide_ subject tables, UCL was ranked in the
top ten in 34 subjects out of 42 offered (81%). It was ranked top for American
studies, linguistics, speech and language therapy, and architecture.[244]

In the 2023 _Guardian University Guide_ subject tables, UCL is ranked top in

American studies, building, information systems and management, liberal arts,
and town and country planning. It is ranked in the top ten for 31 of 44
subjects offered (70%). The 2023 _Good University Guide_ also ranked UCL 98th
in their social inclusion ranking (covering England and Wales). UCL was named
[University of the Year](/wiki/Sunday_Times_University_of_the_Year "Sunday
Times University of the Year") in the _Times/Sunday Times Good University
Guide_ for 2024.[238]

Analysis by the [Department for Education](/wiki/Department_for_Education
"Department for Education") in 2018, found that UCL had an impact on earnings
of graduates five years after graduation of +15.5% for women (7th highest
impact) and +16.2% for men (10th highest impact) compared to average graduates
with similar background characteristics (prior attainment, socio-economic
status, etc.) and subject choice.[245]

Admission to UCL is highly selective with an average entry tariff for 2020–21

UCL since 2015 and the majority of acceptances since 2017. The ratio of main-
scheme applicants to acceptances in 2022 was 10.3 for UK applicants and 9.9

recruiter,[256] with 47.4% of 2022 UK admissions coming from the London region
and a further 28.1% from the adjacent East of England and South East
regions.[251]

Of UCL's young UK domiciled undergraduates, 32.7% were [privately

mainstream British universities.[257]

Test for Law](/wiki/National_Admissions_Test_for_Law "National Admissions Test

are required to take the [Thinking Skills
Assessment](/wiki/Thinking_Skills_Assessment "Thinking Skills Assessment")
(TSA) should they be selected for an assessment day.[258] Medicine, pharmacy
and English also interview undergraduate applicants prior to making an offer
of admission.[258]

UCL runs a contextual offer scheme called Access UCL, whereby eligible
applicants can receive conditional offers for courses at UCL that have lower
requirements than the standard conditional offers for those courses.
Eligibility for Access UCL can be through an applicant living in a deprived
areas or an area with low participation in higher education, through having
spent time in care, though being a young adult carer, or through being
estranged from their family. Applicants must have attended a [state
school](/wiki/State_school "State school"), unless they have spent time in
care. Mature applicants are assessed on the same criteria, and are
additionally not eligible if they have completed or are on the final year of
an undergraduate degree. While the scheme enables applicants from
disadvantaged backgrounds to receive contextual offers, it does not guarantee
that an offer will be made.[262] Contextual offers vary by course. For
example, a contextual offer for the law LLB reduces the requirement from A*AA
to BBB at [A level](/wiki/A_level "A level"),[263] but for the physics MSci
from A*AA to AAB.[264]

UCL also runs week-long UCL Summer Schools for high-achieving students from
disadvantaged backgrounds in partnership with the [Sutton
Trust](/wiki/Sutton_Trust "Sutton Trust"). These give participants the
opportunity to explore London, to develop skills in their chosen subject, to
improve their university applications through personal statement workshops and
talks by admissions tutors, and to take part in social activities.[265]

In 2023, UCL launched an integrated engineering [foundation
year](/wiki/Foundation_year "Foundation year") programme based at UCL East for
disadvantaged students who do not meet the standard entry requirements for the
Faculty of Engineering's undergraduate degrees. Candidates must have attended
UK state schools for [A levels](/wiki/A_level "A level") or equivalent (unless
they have experienced forced displacement) and have experienced specific
socioeconomic or personal circumstances such as time in care, estrangement,
forced displacement, or receipt of free school meals. The programme's academic
entry requirements are based on [UCAS Tariff](/wiki/UCAS_Tariff "UCAS Tariff")
points rather than letter grades.[266]

The university runs intensive one-year [foundation
courses](/wiki/Foundation_programme "Foundation programme"), called
Undergraduate Preparatory Certificates, in either sciences or humanities, for
international students who do not meet the university's requirements for
admission.[267]

For UK domiciled young full-time undergraduate entrants in 2020/21, 67.6% came
from state schools, significantly below the location-adjusted benchmark of
74.5%, and 4.3% came from low participation neighbourhoods, not significantly
different from the location-adjusted benchmark of 4.0%.[268] For UK-domiciled
undergraduate entrants in 2022/23, UCAS data shows no significant difference
in offer rate with ethnicity or gender.[252] Applicants from the 20% of
neighbourhoods with the lowest rates of participation in higher education
receive offers at a rate 4.9% higher than would be expected based on their
subject choice and predicted grades alone, a statistically significant
difference, accounting for 6.3% of all offers. The offer rate for applicants
from the 20% of neighbourhoods with the lowest rates of participation in
higher education is not significantly different from that expected, with
applicants from those neighbourhoods accounting for 48.9% of all offers.[252]

### Students' union

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=University_College_London&action=edit&section=31
"Edit section: Students' union")]

Main article: [Students' Union UCL](/wiki/Students%27_Union_UCL "Students'
Union UCL")

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d0/University_College_London_Union.jpg/250px-
University_College_London_Union.jpg)](/wiki/File:University_College_London_Union.jpg)Students'
union building on Gordon Street

Founded in 1893, Students' Union UCL, formerly the UCL Union, is one of the
oldest students' unions in England, although postdating the [Liverpool Guild
of Students](/wiki/Liverpool_Guild_of_Students "Liverpool Guild of Students")
which formed a student representative council in 1892.[66][269] Students'
Union UCL operates both as the representative voice for UCL students, and as a
provider of a wide range of services. It is democratically controlled through
General Meetings and referendums, and is run by elected student officers. The
union also supports a range of services, including numerous clubs and
societies, sports facilities, an advice service, and a number of bars, cafes
and shops.[270]

As of
2021,[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_College_London&action=edit)
there are over 250 clubs and societies under the umbrella of the UCL
Union.[271] These include: UCL Snowsports (one of the largest sports society
at UCL, responsible for organising the annual UCL ski trip),[272] [Pi
Media](/wiki/UCL_Pi_Media "UCL Pi Media") (responsible for _Pi Magazine_ and
_Pi Newspaper_ , UCL's official student publications),[273] the Debating
Society (established 1829),[274] and the UCL Union Film Society, with past
members including [Christopher Nolan](/wiki/Christopher_Nolan "Christopher
Nolan").[275]

### Faith

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=University_College_London&action=edit&section=32
"Edit section: Faith")]

From its foundation the college has been deliberately secular; the initial
justification for this was that it would enable students of different
Christian traditions (specifically [Roman
Catholics](/wiki/Roman_Catholic_Church "Roman Catholic Church"),
[Anglicans](/wiki/Anglicanism "Anglicanism") and
[Nonconformists](/wiki/Nonconformist_\(Protestantism\) "Nonconformist
\(Protestantism\)")) to study alongside each other without conflict.[276] In
order to cater to people of all faiths, UCL opened a prayer room (with
attached ablution facilities) and a silent meditation room in the student
centre in February 2019, and there is a quiet contemplation room behind 16–26
Gordon Square. There is also a Christian chaplain (who also serves as
interfaith advisor) and there are student societies for most major
religions.[277][278]

### Sport

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=University_College_London&action=edit&section=33
"Edit section: Sport")]

The union runs over 70 sports clubs,[279] including the UCL Cricket Club
(Men's and Women's), [UCL Boat Club](/wiki/University_College_London_Boat_Club
"University College London Boat Club") (Men's and Women's clubs), UCL Running,
Athletics and Cross Country Club,
[Polo](/wiki/University_College_London_Polo_Club "University College London
Polo Club"), and UCL Rugby Club (Men's and Women's), as well as [RUMS sports
clubs](/wiki/UCL_Medical_School#Student_societies "UCL Medical School") for
medical students (from Royal Free, University College and Middlesex, the three
medical schools that merged into UCL).[170][280]

UCL clubs compete in inter-university fixtures in the [British Universities
and Colleges Sport](/wiki/British_Universities_and_Colleges_Sport "British
Universities and Colleges Sport") (BUCS) competition in a range of sports,
including athletics, basketball, cricket, fencing, football, hockey, netball,
rugby union and tennis. In the 2021/22 season, UCL finished in 16th position
in the final BUCS rankings.[281]

UCL sports facilities include a fitness centre at the main UCL campus in
Bloomsbury and a 90-acre (36 ha) athletics ground in [Shenley](/wiki/Shenley
"Shenley"), Hertfordshire,[282] part of which is used as the [Watford Football
Club Training Ground](/wiki/Watford_Football_Club_Training_Ground "Watford
Football Club Training Ground").[283] It also exercises effective control over
[Somers Town](/wiki/Somers_Town,_London "Somers Town, London") Community
Sports Centre, with the power to appoint five of the nine trustees.[2] The
sports centre includes a six-court sports hall,[284] as well as an
activity/dance studio and an all-weather outdoor multi-use games
area.[285][286][287]

### Mascot

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=University_College_London&action=edit&section=34
"Edit section: Mascot")]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2a/Pencil_etching_of_Phineas_Maclino.jpg/60px-
Pencil_etching_of_Phineas_Maclino.jpg)](/wiki/File:Pencil_etching_of_Phineas_Maclino.jpg)Pencil
signed etching of Phineas Maclino

The UCL mascot was Phineas MacLino, or Phineas, a wooden tobacconist's sign of
a kilted Jacobite Highlander stolen from outside a shop in [Tottenham Court
Road](/wiki/Tottenham_Court_Road "Tottenham Court Road") during the
celebrations of the [relief of Ladysmith](/wiki/Relief_of_Ladysmith "Relief of
Ladysmith"), part of the [Second Boer War](/wiki/Second_Boer_War "Second Boer
War"), in March 1900.[288] In 1922, Phineas was stolen by students from
King's, marking the start of 'mascotry', leading to an hour-long battle and
the eventual return of Phineas.[289] In 1993, the students' union's centenary
year, Phineas was placed in the third floor bar of 25 Gordon Street and the
bar named after him.[290] In 2019, the students' union voted to remove the
mascot from the bar due to its links to imperialism and British
colonialism.[291][292]

### Rivalry with King's College London

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=University_College_London&action=edit&section=35
"Edit section: Rivalry with King's College London")]

Main article: [King's College London–UCL
rivalry](/wiki/King%27s_College_London%E2%80%93UCL_rivalry "King's College
London–UCL rivalry")

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a0/UCL-
KCL_Varsity_Rugby_2014.jpg/250px-UCL-
KCL_Varsity_Rugby_2014.jpg)](/wiki/File:UCL-KCL_Varsity_Rugby_2014.jpg)A UCL
player attacks in his team's 2014 Varsity victory. UCL's traditional rivalry
with King's College is nowadays most noticeable at the annual [varsity rugby
game](/wiki/The_London_Varsity "The London Varsity").

UCL has a long-running, mostly friendly rivalry with [King's College
London](/wiki/King%27s_College_London "King's College London"), but there were
frequent clashes in the interwar period which have historically been known as
"rags".[293] UCL students have been referred to by students from King's as the
"Godless Scum of Gower Street", in reference to a comment made at the founding
of King's, which was based on Christian principles. UCL students in turn
referred to King's as "Strand Polytechnic".[294][295]

In 1922 Phineas, the UCL mascot was kidnapped by King's students, leading to a
pitched battle in the King's College quad as UCL students recovered their
mascot.[296][297] Shortly after this, King's adopted their own mascot –
initially a large papier-mâché beer bottle, soon replaced by [Reggie the
Lion](/wiki/King%27s_College_London_Students%27_Union#Mascot "King's College
London Students' Union").[289] During the 1927 rag, Reggie was captured by UCL
students and his body filled with rotten apples. During the same year, an
attempt by King's students to capture Phineas led to the "Battle of Gower
Street", caught on camera by [British Pathé](/wiki/Path%C3%A9_News "Pathé
News").[298] On another occasion, Reggie was castrated by UCL students.[299]

King's students stole the embalmed head of [Jeremy
Bentham](/wiki/Jeremy_Bentham "Jeremy Bentham") in October 1975, only
returning it after UCL paid a ransom to charity. The head is now kept in the
UCL vaults.[300]

### Student campaigns

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=University_College_London&action=edit&section=36
"Edit section: Student campaigns")]

In 1956, UCL students organised a silent march progressing against the Soviet
oppression of the [Hungarian Revolution of
1956](/wiki/Hungarian_Revolution_of_1956 "Hungarian Revolution of 1956").
Around 1,300 students from across institutions in London matches from the
Royal Albert Hall to the Soviet Embassy. There were active [Campaign for
Nuclear Disarmament](/wiki/Campaign_for_Nuclear_Disarmament "Campaign for
Nuclear Disarmament") and [anti-apartheid](/wiki/Anti-Apartheid_Movement
"Anti-Apartheid Movement") students groups at UCL in the 1960s and a
pioneering GaySoc group that helped drive the [National Union of
Students](/wiki/National_Union_of_Students_\(United_Kingdom\) "National Union
of Students \(United Kingdom\)") gay rights campaign in the 1970s. 1977 saw a
student occupation of administrative offices and the Slade School in protest
against government cuts to higher education.[65]

In 2010, protests by students and staff led UCL to promise to pay a [living
wage](/wiki/Living_wage "Living wage") to all UCL staff.[301] As part of the
[protests against the UK government's plans to increase student
fees](/wiki/2010_UK_student_protests "2010 UK student protests"), around 200
students occupied the Jeremy Bentham Room and part of the [Slade School of
Fine Art](/wiki/Slade_School_of_Fine_Art "Slade School of Fine Art") for over
two weeks during November and December 2010.[302][303] The university
successfully obtained a court order to evict the students but stated that it
did not intend to enforce the order if possible.[303]

The late 2010s saw student campaigns around the cost of university-run
accommodation. In 2016, over 1000 students took part in a [rent
strike](/wiki/Rent_strike "Rent strike") in protest against high rents and
poor conditions. Organisers said they had won over £1 million in rent cuts,
freezes and grants from UCL in the settlement that ended the strike.[304]
Another rent strike in 2017 lead to UCL pledging around £1.4 million in
bursaries and rent freezes, mostly in the form of accommodation bursaries for
less well-off students totalling £600,000 per year for the 2017/18 and 2018/19
academic years.[305] Another rent strike was held at two halls of residence in
the third term of the 2017/18 academic year due to complaints over conditions
at those halls.[306]

In 2018, [Aliza Ayaz](/wiki/Aliza_Ayaz "Aliza Ayaz"), then a first year
student founded the university’s first environment student campaign by setting
up the Climate Action Society.[307] The student society led pressure on the
university to divest from fossil fuels and make the announcement
publicly.[308][309]

In 2024, students protesting against the [Gaza war](/wiki/Gaza_war "Gaza war")
set up an [encampment](/wiki/Occupation_\(protest\) "Occupation \(protest\)")
in the campus, emulating the [2024 pro-Palestinian protests](/wiki/2024_pro-
Palestinian_protests_on_university_campuses "2024 pro-Palestinian protests on
university campuses") that took place across universities in the United
States. The UCL encampment followed similar movements by students in other UK
universities, such as the [University of Leeds](/wiki/University_of_Leeds
"University of Leeds") and the [University of
Bristol](/wiki/University_of_Bristol "University of Bristol").[310][311] On 15
November 2024, students protested the visit of Czech Foreign Minister [Jan
Lipavský](/wiki/Jan_Lipavsk%C3%BD "Jan Lipavský"), criticising the Czech
government's support for Israel.[312]

In the 2021/22 academic year, UCL had a total of 46,830 students, of whom
23,800 were undergraduates (11,000 UK, 12,800 international), 16,910 were
taught postgraduates (8,160 UK, 8,745 international) and 6,120 were research
postgraduates (3,520 UK, 2,600 international).[313] In that year, UCL had the
[second-largest total number of students of any university in the United
Kingdom](/wiki/List_of_universities_in_the_United_Kingdom_by_enrolment "List
of universities in the United Kingdom by enrolment") (after the Open
University) and the largest number of postgraduate students; however, in terms
of UK undergraduates it was 68th by size.[313] It had been the UK university
with the highest number of international students every year since
2014/15.[316]

In 2021/22, 87% of UCL's students were full-time and 13% part-time,[313]
although among undergraduates only 3% were part-time. The student body was
split 60.8% female, 39.1% male and 0.1% other gender identity.[313] 24,145 UCL
students (52%) were from outside the UK, of whom 15,795 were from Asia, 4,400
from the [European Union](/wiki/European_Union "European Union"), 1,440 from
[North America](/wiki/North_America "North America"), 890 from elsewhere in
[Europe](/wiki/Europe "Europe"), 790 from the [Middle East](/wiki/Middle_East
"Middle East"), 370 from [Africa](/wiki/Africa "Africa"), 310 from South
America, and 155 from Australasia; 45% of overseas students at UCL – 10,785 –
came from China.[314] Additionally, UCL had 895 students studying wholly
overseas in 2021/22 (10 undergraduate, 785 taught postgraduate and 80 research
postgraduate) that are not included in the count of the student
population.[317]

For UK domiciled students, UCL's student body in 2021/22 was 52.9% white,
26.4% Asian, 7.6% mixed, 6.4% black and 4.6% other, compared to an average
across London institutions of 47.8% white, 22.2% Asian, 6.7% mixed, 15.5%
black and 4.9% other. Over the whole student body, 12.5% had a known
disability, compared to 15.8% across all institutions.[315]

### Diversity

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=University_College_London&action=edit&section=38
"Edit section: Diversity")]

UCL holds an institutional silver [Athena SWAN](/wiki/Athena_SWAN "Athena
SWAN") award. It gained its first institutional award (bronze) in 2006 and was
promoted to silver in 2015. As of November
2021,[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_College_London&action=edit)
21 departments across UCL hold bronze awards, 17 hold silver awards and three
hold gold awards.[318] UCL also holds an institutional bronze Race Equality
Charter award, which it first gained in 2015.[319]

UCL was formerly a member of [Stonewall Diversity
Champions](/wiki/Stonewall_\(charity\)#Diversity_Champions_and_workplace_equality_index
"Stonewall \(charity\)") scheme, promoting LGBT+ equality. It left in February
2020 as a cost-cutting measure and then controversially decided in late 2021
not to rejoin, against the advice of its equality diversity and inclusion
committee, following a vote of the academic board that expressed fears that
membership of the scheme could inhibit academic freedom. The decision not to
rejoin was strongly opposed by staff and student LGBT+ groups at UCL and by
the students' union.[320][321]
